summary:
Aceh operates a provincial sharia criminal code alongside the national criminal code. Special autonomy granted in 2005 authorised the introduction of Islamic criminal law for Muslim residents, and Qanun Aceh Nomor 6 Tahun 2014 tentang Hukum Jinayat has been enforced since 23 October 2015. The code's provisions are applied to anyone present in the province, including foreign visitors, so a trans traveller's exposure does not depend on religion or residency.

Article 63 of the Qanun defines liwath as sexual acts between males and Article 64 defines musahaqah as sexual acts between females, each determined by birth sex. Both offences carry up to 100 lashes, up to 100 months' imprisonment, or a fine of up to 1,000 grams of gold. Because the definitions turn on birth sex rather than current presentation or documents, a trans visitor whose identity papers, appearance or partner are read as same-sex conduct falls inside the offence.

The provisions were first applied on 23 May 2017, when an Islamic court in Banda Aceh had two men publicly caned with 82 lashes each for gay sex before hundreds of spectators outside a mosque. Two men aged 20 and 23 were sentenced to public caning for same-sex relations the same year, and several further cases of men publicly caned after guilty findings followed.

On 11 August 2025 a sharia court sentenced two men aged 20 and 21 to public caning for kissing, following an April arrest in which police broke into a toilet. The caning was reported on 26 August 2025. Public caning is the province's standing punishment for sharia offences.

Enforcement against transgender women in Aceh has taken a different form. In January 2018 police in North Aceh arrested twelve transgender women, forcibly cut their hair, compelled them to wear men's clothing and closed their beauty salons. Accounts of a January 2018 parlour raid in the province describe officers shaving the heads of transgender women, stripping their shirts and bras and parading them in the street while forcing them to shout that they would become men.

Legal scholarship from Aceh's Islamic university analyses a rising number of waria cases in Banda Aceh through the lens of sharia law enforcement, indicating that enforcement against transgender women in the province is an ongoing subject of local legal study rather than an isolated episode.
tangentialFactors:
Aceh's sharia code sits alongside the national criminal code rather than replacing it, so conduct in the province can be pursued under either layer, and the provincial religious courts impose caning as a public sentence.

The documented pattern in Aceh separates by target. Men convicted of same-sex conduct are caned under the sharia code, while transgender women have been met with raids, forced haircuts and clothing changes, and the closure of their businesses.
localsOnly:
For residents, the 2005 autonomy grant frames the sharia code as applying to Muslim residents, and the provincial religious court system is the forum for these offences.

The January 2018 closure of beauty salons in North Aceh removed a documented source of income for transgender women in the province. Local research links the position of waria in Banda Aceh to social exclusion and enforcement pressure.
outOfScopeNotes:
No case in the sources records a transgender person in Aceh charged under Article 63 or Article 64; the documented caning convictions involve men.

Survey evidence on violence against transgender women in Indonesia is not disaggregated to Aceh, so a province-level rate is not sourced.

One source describes Aceh as the only province criminalising same-sex relations; the national assessment identifies a second province as also criminalising it. The discrepancy is unresolved.

The Aceh legal-scholarship item is available only as a citation with title and keywords; its findings on the number and handling of waria cases could not be verified in detail.

Whether the caning reported on 26 August 2025 and the 11 August 2025 sentencing refer to the same case is not resolved by the sources.
